summary.title: OSNOISE Tracer
summary.one_liner: The Linux osnoise tracer measures how much OS and hardware interference a spinning thread suffers and attributes each noise event to NMI, IRQ, SoftIRQ, thread, or hardware sources.
takeaways: osnoise runs a loop with preemption, SoftIRQs and IRQs enabled and counts interference from NMI, IRQ, SoftIRQ and thread sources per CPU.
Noise not attributed to any OS-level source is counted as hardware noise, which is how VM host interference shows up.
Enable it by writing 'osnoise' to current_tracer in the tracefs directory (usually /sys/kernel/tracing) and read the trace file.
Tune behavior with osnoise/cpus, period_us, runtime_us, stop_tracing_us, and options such as OSNOISE_WORKLOAD and OSNOISE_IRQ_DISABLE.
Tracepoints osnoise:nmi_noise, irq_noise, softirq_noise, thread_noise and sample_threshold give per-event durations, with nested noise subtracted to avoid double counting.
summary.summary: This kernel documentation page explains the osnoise tracer, which builds on the hwlat_detector approach to measure operating system noise seen by a thread in high-performance computing contexts. The tracer runs a loop with interrupts, SoftIRQs and preemption enabled, and records entry and exit of each interference source, reporting total noise, maximum single noise, CPU availability and per-source counters at the end of each period. The page covers usage through tracefs, a sample trace output with field definitions, configuration files, tracer options, and tracepoints with an example trace. It also notes that tracepoint durations are net values and that the tracer can run without its workload to measure arbitrary Linux tasks.
